title: Carney to deliver speech at federalist rally in Calgary ahead of Alberta referendum

image.caption: Carney greets students during a visit to the University of Calgary. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)

items: October 16Carney's day in CalgaryCarney greets students during a visit to the University of Calgary. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)I'm Kelsea Arnett, a reporter based in Calgary. Ahead of tonight's rally, Carney toured the city to rally Albertans to vote to stay in Canada. He shook hands with community leaders, local business owners and some eager students at the University of Calgary — including one who asked the prime minister to sign his chest. (Carney declined.)

How the pro-Canadian side is feelingAlex BoydA supporter of the pro-Canada group Forever Canadian in Calgary on Oct. 9. (Ahmed Zakot/Reuters)I'm Alex Boyd, a political affairs reporter at CBC Calgary. I'm headed to the rally tonight with the hope of chatting with as many federalist supporters as I can. We've heard again and again that separatist supporters would "crawl over broken glass" to vote (thank you to former premier Jason Kenney for popularizing that one), but I'm curious how the federalist side is feeling as we head into the final days of this campaign. There's a general sense that the energy has shifted a bit in recent weeks — the pro-Canadian side has begun to raise more money, there are more Canadian flags on cars and front lawns — but there's no question this has been an emotional debate on both sides. Into that comes the prime minister, who also happens to be an Albertan.

The final pushJennifer KeillerA pro-separation sign in the window of a cafe in Coutts, Alta., on Wednesday. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)I'm Jen Keiller, a reporter in the Calgary newsroom. We're officially heading into the campaign home stretch, with Carney's appearances part of what will be a busy weekend of campaigning. Carney will make a campaign stop with Premier Danielle Smith Friday morning at a brewery in Red Deer. The pro-separation group Let Alberta Decide has a rally outside the legislature on Saturday afternoon.Then on Sunday, the Alberta Federation of Labour will rally in the same spot to encourage people to vote to remain.

The Canadian PressAlberta Premier Danielle Smith speaks during a news conference in Calgary on May 22. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)Alberta Premier Danielle Smith wants citizens to vote yes to the nine provincial autonomy and immigration questions, but vote for Alberta to remain a province."Canada can still work," she said after voting. "We just need to make some changes."Polls have suggested a strong majority of Albertans want to remain in Canada, but the debate has at times been acrimonious, dividing families and neighbours.

Political leaders push for Alberta to stay a province, with advance polling well underwayThe Canadian PressAlberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi leaves after casting his referendum vote at an advance polling station in Calgary on Tuesday. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)Advance voting began Tuesday and ends Saturday. Elections Alberta said the first day was a busy one, with close to 175,000 voters trekking to the polls.Michelle Gurney, a spokesperson for the agency, said Tuesday's turnout was higher than the daily average of nearly 152,000 people seen during the advance voting period in the 2023 provincial election.Elections Alberta has said it's expecting record voter turnout for the referendum, and it saw unprecedented interest in mail-in ballot requests last month.Gurney said Wednesday that nearly two-thirds of the roughly 658,000 special ballots requested have now been returned ahead of Friday's 5 p.m. deadline.Opposition NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi was among those who voted Tuesday. He encouraged Albertans to reject the United Conservative Party government's nine proposals and vote to stay in Canada.

October 15Oct. 19 referendum includes 10 questionsJohn MazerolleVoting in the Alberta referendum? Experts say do your homeworkAs Albertans prepare to vote in the upcoming referendum, experts are raising concerns over the complex and potentially confusing wording on the ballot. For The National, CBC’s Ashley Fraser breaks down the questions and how voters can prepare before heading to the polls.There are actually 10 questions being put to a vote next week, with the question of whether Alberta should remain a province of Canada or hold a second, binding referendum being No. 10.That question is being put to Albertans because Alberta Premier Danielle Smith promised a separation vote if citizens gathered the required number of citizens on a petition, which they did. The other nine questions come directly from the provincial government.Smith announced the referendum in mid-February, saying she trusts the judgment of Albertans.Five of the other questions deal with immigration, proposing that the province take more control over immigration from the federal government, limiting non-permanent residents' eligibility to public and social services and asking if voters should be required to show proof of citizenship in order to vote in a provincial election.Other questions include whether Alberta should work with the governments of other willing provinces on these changes: selecting their own justices for the King's Bench and Appeal courts; abolishing the Senate; allowing provinces to opt out of federal programs "that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services"; and giving provincial laws standing over federal laws in shared areas of jurisdiction. – With files from CBC Calgary and The Canadian Press

Carney to attend Forever Canadian rally in CalgaryJohn MazerolleCarney says Canada is 'worth fighting for' ahead of Alberta independence voteIn a video released on Thanksgiving Monday, Prime Minister Mark Carney called for national unity as Albertans prepare to vote next week in a referendum on the province's future in Canada.Prime Minister Mark Carney will be in Calgary tonight to attend a Forever Canadian rally tour days before a referendum asking Albertans if they should stay in Canada or hold another, binding referendum on separating. Forever Canadian founder Thomas Lukaszuk, who extended the invitation to Carney in a social media post on Monday, says Carney's decision to come to the rallies is a good sign for the movement."At the end of the day, Albertans would want to hear from him," Lukaszuk said. The announcement comes after Carney made a Thanksgiving address to Albertans from his alma mater in west Edmonton. In the video, he said Canada is facing threats to its economy but that in spite of them, the country is continuing to grow."Generations of Albertans helped build this country," Carney said. "It's yours, it's ours and it's worth fighting for."– With files from CBC Calgary
